newsitem.title: USA: Colorado lawmakers eye $140 mln taxpayer rebate.
newsitem.headline: Colorado lawmakers eye $140 mln taxpayer rebate.

text.p: Colorado, whose economic boom produced a surprise $140 million windfall in the fiscal year that just ended, now is weighing how that money might be returned to taxpayers, the state controller said Tuesday.

Clifford Hall, who was in Boston for a National Association of State Auditors, Comptrollers and Treasurers conference, told Reuters in an interview that this was the first year a constitutional amendment enacted a few years ago to limit the state's revenues would take effect.
The new law, which also restricts the state's expenditures, requires extra funds over a certain limit to be repaid to voters unless they approve letting the state keep their money.
"In 1996-1997, the state breached the revenue limit for the first time," said Hall.

"Early in the year, it was assumed that we would not breach the limit, and that the economy would tail off a little bit," he explained later. "But it never happened; the rest of the economy stayed strong for whole year."

Although Colorado's economy has diversified from its traditional strength in oil and mining and into services, for example, the state has been enjoying a boom, with unemployment slipping to nearly a 24-year low of about 3.7 percent.

The extra surplus under the new rule, called Amendment Number One, mainly comes from personal income tax collections, which rose almost 11 perecent from the 1996 fiscal year, and sales tax revenues, which climbed 7.5 percent.

The windfall surpassed early predictions that it would total from $20 million to $50 million, Hall noted. The state's 1997 fiscal year ended on August 1, and while the final numbers were not due for two weeks or so, in late June, the year-end General Fund balance was estimated at $385 million.

Gov. Roy Romer initially considered calling a special legislative session to explore keeping the big windfall in order to spend it on roads and education, Hall said. But the Democrat governor ran into resistance from both Republican houses, he explained, and now Romer is weighing whether to call a special session in August to see how Colorado might return the money to its citizens.
Alternatively, the governor might decide to wait until the regular session, which runs from January through May, resumes in 1998.

And lawmakers still could recommend that the state get the voters' approval to hang onto the funds, as the only deadline is June 30, 1998, when the surplus has to be returned unless a bid to override the amendment has succeeded.

The options for rebating the money, which would work out to around $80 if divided equally among the state's approximately 3.8 million residents, include repaying all income tax filers, or more narrowly, sending checks only to those who paid income taxes, which would knock out those who had a negative income tax, the state controller said.
Looking ahead, he added the Romer Administration again was predicting the economy might ease a bit.

A softening in residential construction, as fewer people are moving to Colorado and what appeared to be the end of a big wave of home-buying by baby boomers, might signal slower growth in fiscal 1998.
